newsitem.title: UK: Sterling debt and futures closing report.
newsitem.headline: Sterling debt and futures closing report.

text.p: Gilts subsided weakly into the weekend having recovered after a robust set of GDP data early on Friday morning. The June gilt future settled 9/32 lower at 108-24. It dropped to 108-22 after official data showed first quarter GDP up 3.0 percent year-on-year. Thereafter it clawed back up to 108-29 before sliding again, late in the European day.
Dealers said with the gilt/Bund spread now at 192 basis points, gilts should not fall much further.
"Volumes have been thin but I haven't seen a single seller all day," said a senior salesman at a UK brokerage.

The contract traded a paltry 35,000 contracts. The salesman said he saw buyers in the cash market. "And when we looked for stock in the market this afternoon, we couldn't find any. That gives me the impression that at 193 over Bunds, the market makers want to hold on to their stock," he said. First quarter GDP data, showing above-trend growth, added to fears that interest rates may head higher soon after next week's election.
Short sterling still bore the scars at the end of the session. The June contract settled two basis points lower at 93.34, discounting a half-point rate rise within two months.
September is factoring a further quarter point rise. It settled at 93.06, down 0.03.

"The figures demonstrate that the economy remained buoyant during the first quarter," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc. "They do provide another argument for a degree of overall policy restraint."

But the recovery remains skewed. The breakdown of the figures showed the service sector storming ahead, up 3.9 percent year-on-year while the hard-pressed manufacturing industries grew only slightly faster than the fourth quarter, the ONS said.
Next week is all about Thursday's election for the gilt market, at least that is until U.S. non-farm payrolls are released on Friday.
The market should cruise comfortably through as long as Labour maintains a healthy lead in the opinion polls, avoiding the nightmare scenario of a hung parliament.

There was a sharp intake of breath earlier this week when one poll slashed Labour's lead to five points from 14. But others since have put the opposition between 15 and 21 points ahead, pointing to a Labour lansdlide.
